the ways in which the Mexican State, in collaboration with the World Bank and other international organizations, has used cash transfers as a means to transform rural life.

the ways in which multilateral banks, national states, and the people who live in the territories of the states they govern are linked in the process of implementing social policies, in this case, cash transfers.

the ways that the Mexican state has sought to support a counterfactual futurity, a futurity that is based on the assumption that a rural to urban migration, the conversion of children from peasant to urban life, and the monetization of rural life will bring about progress and development in Mexico.

Progresa Oportuniades is not a social welfare program but a social engineering program.

, in the Mexican case, the implementation of cash transfer programs was part of a long term strategy of structural adjustment that aimed to facilitate a long term adjustment to a new reality in which the rural sector was no longer the main provider of jobs and the main source of economic growth, but rather a place to be left behind.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, instead of breaking the intergenerational cycle of reproduction of poverty, the Mexican cash transfer programs Progresa Oporitundades (1994) and Oportunidades (2002) were designed to facilitate a long term structural adjustment, keep rural-urban migration constant, convert peasant children to new economic activities, monetize the rural economy, encourage new forms of political leadership and eradicate the traditional "caciquismo".
the Oportunidades program was not designed to break the cycle of intergenerational reproduction of poverty, but instead, to facilitate a long-term structural adjustment.

we have been able to show that the Mexican government's cash transfer programs were not implemented to break the intergenerational reproduction of poverty, as they are commonly understood, but to facilitate a long-term structural adjustment and to maintain a constant migration from rural to urban areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the "counterfactual" is a powerful tool for the multilateral banks and Mexican state to justify their own existence.
the Mexican government, with support from the World Bank, has used the counterfactual to justify the expansion and consolidation of a neoliberal model of development.
